units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Laws of exponents
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Mathematics, Term 1: Exponents (laws of exponents for integral exponents; simplify expressions; solve simple exponential equations)
units.intention: Today I am using the laws of exponents to simplify expressions.
units.prompt: Which law do you find easiest to remember, and why?

lesson.say: When multiplying powers with the same base, add the exponents. When dividing, subtract them. x to the 3 times x to the 4 is x to the 7.
lesson.html:
aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ→aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ

Only works when the base is the same.

lesson.say: A power raised to another power: multiply the exponents. x squared, all cubed, is x to the 6.
lesson.html:
(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ→(ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ

Every factor inside the bracket gets the exponent.

lesson.say: Anything except zero to the power of zero is one. A negative exponent means one over the positive power. Two to the minus three is one over eight.
lesson.html:
a⁰ = 1→a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ→2⁻³ = 1/8

A negative exponent does not make the answer negative.

example.q: Simplify (2x³)² × x⁻⁴.
steps: (2x³)² = 4x⁶.
4x⁶ × x⁻⁴: add the exponents, 6 + (−4) = 2.
Answer: 4x².

questions.q: Simplify: a⁵ × a³
questions.explain: a⁵ × a³ = a⁸.

questions.q: Simplify: y¹⁰ ÷ y⁴
questions.explain: y¹⁰ ÷ y⁴ = y⁶.

questions.q: What is 5⁰?
hints: Any non-zero number to the power 0.

questions.q: What is 3⁻²?
Solve: 2ˣ = 32

options: Checking the base is the same

units.parent: Your child used the laws of exponents to simplify expressions and solve simple exponential equations.
units.teacher: Shows applying exponent laws, zero and negative exponents, and solving exponential equations with a common base.
units.done: Same base: add when multiplying, subtract when dividing, multiply for a power of a power.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Trigonometric ratios
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Mathematics, Term 2: Trigonometry (define sin, cos and tan in right-angled triangles; solve two-dimensional problems)
units.intention: Today I am using sin, cos and tan to work with right-angled triangles.
units.prompt: How do you decide which ratio to use?

lesson.say: Choose an angle, called theta. The hypotenuse is the longest side. The opposite side is across from theta. The adjacent side is next to theta.
lesson.html: Labels depend on which angle you choose.

lesson.say: Sine theta is opposite over hypotenuse. Cosine theta is adjacent over hypotenuse. Tangent theta is opposite over adjacent. Remember SOH CAH TOA.
lesson.html:
sin θ = O/H→cos θ = A/H→tan θ = O/A

SOH CAH TOA

lesson.say: In this triangle, sine theta is three fifths, cosine theta is four fifths, and tangent theta is three quarters.
lesson.html:
sin θ = 3/5→cos θ = 4/5→tan θ = 3/4

Use a calculator in degree mode to find angles and lengths.

example.q: A ramp is 10 m long and rises at 30°. How high does it rise?
steps: The ramp is the hypotenuse, 10 m. The height is opposite the 30° angle.
Opposite and hypotenuse: use sin.

questions.q: Which ratio is opposite over hypotenuse?
questions.explain: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse.

questions.q: In the triangle shown, what is tan θ?
questions.html: <svg width="190" height="140" viewBox="0 0 190 140" role="img" aria-label="Right-angled triangle with angle theta at the bottom left. Opposite side 3, adjacent side 4, hypotenuse 5."><polygon points="20,120 170,120 170,20" fill="var(--brand-soft)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="156" y="106" width="14" height="14" fill="none" stroke="var(--ink)"/><text x="40" y="116" font-size="13" fill="var(--ink)">θ</text><text x="95" y="136" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink)">adjacent 4</text><text x="178" y="72" font-size="13" fill="var(--ink)">3</text><text x="80" y="62" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink)">hyp 5</text></svg>
questions.explain: tan θ = 3/4.

questions.q: You know the adjacent side and the hypotenuse. Which ratio do you use?
questions.explain: cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse.

questions.q: sin θ = 0,5. What is θ, in degrees?
A ladder 6 m long makes 60° with the ground. How far is its foot from the wall?

units.parent: Your child used sin, cos and tan to find sides and angles in right-angled triangles.
units.teacher: Shows labelling sides relative to an angle, selecting the correct ratio and solving 2-D problems.
units.done: Label the sides, choose the ratio with SOH CAH TOA, then solve.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Mean, median and spread
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Mathematics, Term 4: Statistics (measures of central tendency; range, quartiles and interquartile range; five-number summary)
units.intention: Today I am summarising data using averages and spread.
units.prompt: When is the median a better average than the mean?

lesson.say: The mean adds all values and divides by how many there are. The median is the middle value when the data is in order. The mode is the most common value.
lesson.html:
Mean: add ÷ count→Median: middle→Mode: most often

Data: 2, 3, 3, 5, 7. Mean 4, median 3, mode 3.

lesson.say: An outlier is a value far from the rest. It pulls the mean towards it, but barely moves the median. That is why the median is often used for incomes and house prices.
lesson.html:
3, 4, 4, 5, 34

Mean = 10, but the median = 4 describes the data better.

lesson.say: The range is the highest minus the lowest. Quartiles split ordered data into four equal parts. The interquartile range is Q3 minus Q1, the spread of the middle half.
lesson.html:
Min→Q1→Median→Q3→Max

This is the five-number summary.

example.q: Test marks: 45, 52, 58, 61, 64, 70, 88. Find the median and range.
steps: The data is already in order, with 7 values.
The middle value is the 4th: 61.

questions.q: Find the mean of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
Find the median of 9, 2, 7, 4, 5.
questions.explain: In order: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9. The median is 5.

questions.q: What is the mode of 3, 5, 5, 6, 8, 5, 2?
questions.explain: 5 appears most often.

questions.q: Salaries in a small company: R8 000, R9 000, R9 500, R10 000, R95 000. Which average is most representative?
hints: The mean will be pulled up.
questions.explain: The median (R9 500) is not distorted by the outlier.

questions.q: Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 30. What is the interquartile range?

units.parent: Your child summarised data with mean, median, mode, range and quartiles.
units.teacher: Shows calculating measures of central tendency and dispersion, and judging which average represents data best.
units.done: Use averages for the centre and range or IQR for the spread.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Budgets that balance
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Mathematical Literacy: Finance (financial documents; income, expenditure, profit and loss; household budgets)
units.intention: Today I am planning a budget so that income covers expenses.
units.prompt: Which household expense is easiest to cut, and why?

lesson.say: Income is money coming in, like a wage, a grant or money from selling. Expenses are money going out, like transport, food and airtime.
lesson.html:
Income: money in→Expenses: money out

A budget plans how income will cover expenses.

lesson.say: Fixed expenses stay the same each month, like rent or school fees. Variable expenses change, like food, electricity and transport.
lesson.html:
Fixed: rent, school fees→Variable: food, electricity

Variable expenses are usually where you can save.

lesson.say: Subtract total expenses from total income. If the answer is positive, it is a surplus you can save. If it is negative, it is a deficit: you must spend less or earn more.
lesson.html:
Income − expenses = balance

Positive: surplus. Negative: deficit.

example.q: Thabo earns R6 500 a month. He spends R2 800 on rent, R1 900 on food, R950 on transport and R400 on airtime. What is his balance?
steps: Subtract from income: 6 500 − 6 050 = R450.
He has a surplus of R450 to save.

questions.q: Which of these is income?
hints: Which one brings money to the household?
questions.explain: A grant is money coming in. The others are expenses.

questions.q: Which is a fixed expense?
hints: Fixed means the same every month.
Which one is agreed in advance?
questions.explain: Rent stays the same each month. The others change.

questions.q: Lerato's income is R8 200. Her expenses add up to R7 650. What is her surplus, in rand?
A family's income is R12 000 and their expenses are R12 600. What does this mean?
options: They have a deficit of R600
They have a surplus of R600
hints: Are the expenses more or less than the income?
questions.explain: They spend R600 more than they earn: a deficit.

questions.q: A spaza shop buys 24 cold drinks for R168 and sells each one for R10. What is the profit, in rand?
questions.explain: Sales R240 − cost R168 = R72 profit.

options: Sorting money in and money out

units.parent: Your child worked out a household budget: income, fixed and variable expenses, and a surplus or deficit.
units.teacher: Shows identifying income and expenditure, classifying fixed and variable costs, and calculating a budget balance and profit.
units.done: Income minus expenses shows a surplus or a deficit.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Converting units and recipes
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Mathematical Literacy: Measurement (conversions between metric units; measuring length, mass and volume; scaling recipes)
units.intention: Today I am converting between units and scaling a recipe.
units.prompt: Where at home do you see measurements every day?

lesson.say: Length uses millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres. Mass uses grams and kilograms. Volume uses millilitres and litres.
lesson.html:
10 mm = 1 cm→100 cm = 1 m→1 000 m = 1 km

1 000 g = 1 kg and 1 000 ml = 1 ℓ.

lesson.say: To change to a smaller unit, multiply. To change to a bigger unit, divide. Two and a half kilograms is 2 500 grams.
lesson.html:
To a smaller unit: ×→To a bigger unit: ÷

2,5 kg × 1 000 = 2 500 g

lesson.say: To feed more people, multiply every ingredient by the same number. If a recipe serves 4 and you need to feed 12, multiply everything by 3.
lesson.html:
12 ÷ 4 = 3→every ingredient × 3

Scale every ingredient by the same number.

example.q: A recipe for 6 people uses 750 g of mealie meal. How much is needed for 18 people, in kilograms?
steps: 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so multiply by 3.

questions.q: How many millilitres are in 2 litres?
Convert 350 cm to metres.
To change kilometres to metres, you …
questions.explain: 1 km = 1 000 m, so multiply by 1 000.

questions.q: A recipe for 4 people needs 300 ml of milk. How many millilitres are needed for 10 people?
hints: Find the amount for 1 person first.
questions.explain: 75 ml per person × 10 = 750 ml.

questions.q: Which is the heaviest?
questions.explain: 2,1 kg = 2 100 g, more than 2 050 g and 1 900 g.

options: Finding the amount for one person

units.parent: Your child converted between metric units and scaled a recipe for more people.
units.teacher: Shows converting between metric units of length, mass and volume, and using proportional reasoning to scale recipes.
units.done: To a smaller unit, multiply. To a bigger unit, divide.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Map scales and grids
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Mathematical Literacy: Maps, plans and other representations (number and bar scales; grid references; estimating real distances on maps)
units.intention: Today I am using a map scale to work out real distances.
units.prompt: When have you used a map, on paper or on a phone?

lesson.say: A scale of 1 to 50 000 means 1 centimetre on the map stands for 50 000 centimetres in real life. That is 500 metres.
lesson.html:
1 cm on the map→50 000 cm real→= 500 m

Scale is written 1 : 50 000.

lesson.say: A bar scale is a line marked with real distances. Measure on the map with a ruler or a piece of string, then compare it with the bar.
lesson.html: A bar scale stays correct when a map is made bigger or smaller, because the bar changes size with it.

lesson.say: Many maps have a grid, with letters along one side and numbers along the other. B3 means column B, row 3. It helps you find places quickly.
lesson.html: Letter: column→Number: row→B3

example.q: On a map with scale 1 : 25 000, two villages are 8 cm apart. How far apart are they really, in kilometres?

questions.q: Scale 1 : 100. A wall is 5 cm long on the plan. How long is it really, in metres?
Scale 1 : 50 000. Two towns are 4 cm apart on the map. What is the real distance, in kilometres?
Why does a bar scale stay correct when a map is photocopied larger?
options: The bar is enlarged by the same amount as the map
The bar is always 1 cm long
hints: What happens to the bar when the map grows?
questions.explain: The bar grows with the map, so it still matches.

questions.q: On a grid map, what does D2 mean?
hints: Letters and numbers label the grid.
questions.explain: D is the column and 2 is the row.

questions.q: A map scale is 1 : 200 000. Which is true?
options: 1 cm on the map is 2 km in real life
1 cm on the map is 200 m
1 cm on the map is 20 km
1 cm on the map is 200 km
Converting cm to m to km
Using the grid letters and numbers

units.parent: Your child used map scales and grid references to work out real distances.
units.teacher: Shows using number and bar scales to calculate real distances, converting units, and reading grid references.
units.done: Measure on the map, multiply by the scale, then change to sensible units.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Surveys and summaries
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Mathematical Literacy: Data handling (developing questions; collecting data with surveys; organising data in frequency tables; mean, median, mode and range)
units.intention: Today I am collecting data and summarising it.
units.prompt: What question would you like to ask your class?

lesson.say: Data handling starts with a question, like how do learners in our class get to school? Then you collect the answers, organise them, summarise them and say what they mean.
lesson.html: Question→Collect→Organise→Summarise→Interpret

lesson.say: A tally mark records each answer. Group tallies in fives so they are easy to count. The frequency is how many times each answer came up.
lesson.html:
Walk: 13 · Taxi: 9 · Bus: 6 · Car: 2

Total: 30 learners.

lesson.say: The mode is the most common answer. For numbers, the mean and median describe the centre, and the range describes the spread. Always say what the numbers mean in real life.
lesson.html: Mode: most common→Mean: fair share→Range: spread

example.q: Five learners' travel times in minutes: 10, 15, 15, 20, 40. Find the mean and the range.
steps: Mean = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 minutes.
Range = 40 − 10 = 30 minutes.

questions.q: Which is the best survey question?
options: How do you usually travel to school?
Don't you think taxis are dangerous?
hints: It doesn't push people towards an answer.
The first one is fair to every answer.
questions.explain: It is clear and doesn't suggest an answer.

questions.q: A tally group of four lines with a fifth line across them stands for how many?
hints: Four lines plus the one across.
questions.explain: Tallies are grouped in fives.

questions.q: Walk 13, Taxi 9, Bus 6, Car 2. What is the mode?
hints: The mode is the most common.
questions.explain: Walking has the highest frequency, 13.

questions.q: Walk 13, Taxi 9, Bus 6, Car 2. How many learners were asked?
Find the range of these prices: R12, R18, R9, R25, R15.

units.parent: Your child asked a survey question, organised the answers in a table and summarised them.
units.teacher: Shows formulating unbiased questions, using tallies and frequency tables, and calculating mode, mean and range in context.
units.done: Ask a fair question, organise the answers, then summarise what they mean.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: How likely is it?
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Mathematical Literacy: Probability (the probability scale from 0 to 1; expressing probability as fractions, decimals and percentages; weather forecasts and games)
units.intention: Today I am describing how likely things are.
units.prompt: What does a 60% chance of rain make you decide to do?

lesson.say: Probability says how likely something is, from 0, impossible, to 1, certain. A half, or 50 percent, means it is just as likely to happen as not.
lesson.html: 0: impossible→0,5: even chance→1: certain

lesson.say: Sometimes every outcome is equally likely. Then the probability is the number of outcomes you want, divided by the total number of outcomes. Rolling a 6 on a dice is 1 out of 6.
lesson.html:
Probability = outcomes you want ÷ all outcomes

P(rolling a 6) = 1/6

lesson.say: You can write a probability as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage. One quarter is 0.25, which is 25 percent. A forecast of 70 percent rain means rain is likely, not certain.
lesson.html: 1/4→0,25→25%

example.q: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green sweets. You take one without looking. What is the probability that it is blue?
steps: Total sweets: 3 + 5 + 2 = 10.
Blue sweets: 5 out of 10.

questions.q: The forecast says there is an 80% chance of rain. What does this mean?
options: Rain is likely, but not certain
It will rain for 80% of the day
questions.explain: 80% means rain is likely, but it might not rain.

questions.q: What is the probability of rolling an even number on a normal dice?
questions.explain: 3 even numbers out of 6 = 1/2.

questions.q: A coin is tossed. What is the probability of heads, as a percentage? (Type the number only.)
Which event has a probability of 0?
options: Rolling a 7 on a normal dice
questions.explain: A normal dice has no 7, so it is impossible.

questions.q: A box has 4 winning tickets and 16 losing tickets. What is the chance of winning?
questions.explain: 4 winners out of 20 tickets = 1/5.

units.parent: Your child described how likely events are, using fractions, decimals and percentages.
units.teacher: Shows using the probability scale, calculating simple theoretical probability, and interpreting forecasts.
units.done: Probability = outcomes you want ÷ all outcomes, from 0 to 1.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Poem: Rank
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 English Home Language: Literature (poetry: imagery, metaphor, enjambment, tone, theme; contextual questions)
units.intention: Today I am analysing how a poet creates meaning through imagery and structure.
units.prompt: What do you think the poem is saying about the workers?
units.passage:
Rank (a 2to.iQ poem)

At five the rank is already awake,
a throat of engines clearing
the night from its voice.

Gogo Nomsa sells boiled eggs and patience,
her hands a quiet arithmetic
of coins and change and small talk.

The queue unspools like thread from a spool,
each worker stitched
to a city that never learns their names.

And still they laugh. And still
the hooter's two short notes
are a kind of song.

lesson.say: Read the poem, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Rank (a 2to.iQ poem)

At five the rank is already awake,
a throat of engines clearing
the night from its voice.

Gogo Nomsa sells boiled eggs and patience,
her hands a quiet arithmetic
of coins and change and small talk.

The queue unspools like thread from a spool,
each worker stitched
to a city that never learns their names.

And still they laugh. And still
the hooter's two short notes
are a kind of song.

lesson.say: The rank is a throat of engines clearing the night from its voice. The rank is personified as a person waking up. Gogo Nomsa sells boiled eggs and patience, which mixes something concrete with something abstract.
lesson.html:
throat of engines→eggs and patience→a quiet arithmetic

Unexpected pairings make us look again.

lesson.say: Enjambment is when a sentence runs over the end of a line without punctuation. It creates flow, like the moving queue. The theme is the dignity and resilience of workers in a city that overlooks them.
lesson.html:
Enjambment: each worker stitched / to a city …

Theme: dignity and resilience.

example.q: What does the simile The queue unspools like thread from a spool suggest?
steps: Thread unspools steadily and continuously.
The queue moves forward in a long, steady line.
It also links to stitched, suggesting workers are sewn into the city's fabric.

questions.q: What figure of speech is a throat of engines clearing the night from its voice?
hints: Does a rank have a throat?
Human qualities given to a place.
questions.explain: The rank is described as a person clearing its throat.

questions.q: Why might the poet say she sells boiled eggs and patience?
options: She is patient with customers as well as selling food
hints: What does she give customers besides eggs?
questions.explain: It suggests she offers patience along with her goods.

questions.q: What does a city that never learns their names suggest?
questions.explain: The workers are essential but unnoticed.

questions.q: What is the tone of the final stanza?
questions.explain: And still they laugh shows resilience and hope.

questions.q: What is enjambment?
options: A sentence running on past the end of a line
A rhyme at the end of a line
hints: No punctuation at the line end.
questions.explain: Enjambment carries a sentence over a line break.

reflect.q: How did you understand the poem best?
options: Unpacking one image at a time

units.parent: Your child analysed a poem's imagery, structure, tone and theme.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting personification, metaphor and simile, enjambment, tone and theme in an unseen poem.
units.done: Look at imagery, structure and tone to find a poem's theme.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Reading visual texts
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 English Home Language: Reading and Viewing (visual literacy: advertisements and cartoons; layout, font, colour, target audience, purpose)
units.intention: Today I am analysing how pictures and words work together in adverts and cartoons.
units.prompt: Which advert has persuaded you recently, and how?

lesson.say: Visual texts combine images and words. Look at the layout, font size, colour, the main image, the slogan and the logo.
lesson.html:
Image→Slogan→Font→Colour→Layout→Logo

Ask: what do I notice first, and why?

lesson.say: Every advert targets an audience and has a purpose: to sell, inform or change behaviour. Colours, models and language are chosen for that audience.
lesson.html:
Who is it for?→What does it want?→How does it persuade?

A sports drink advert might use bold colours and action shots for young athletes.

lesson.say: Cartoons comment on issues, often with humour or exaggeration. Caricature exaggerates features. Speech bubbles, captions and symbols carry the message.
lesson.html:
💬 🖋️

Ask: what is the cartoonist criticising?

example.q: An advert shows a smiling family around a braai with the slogan Real meat, real moments. Who is the target audience and what is the message?
steps: The image shows families and a South African tradition.
The slogan links the product to togetherness.
It targets parents and suggests the product creates family moments.

questions.q: What is a slogan?
questions.explain: A slogan is a short, memorable phrase.

questions.q: Why are the largest words usually the most important?
questions.explain: Size directs attention.

questions.q: What is caricature?
questions.explain: Caricature exaggerates features for effect.

questions.q: An energy drink advert uses neon colours and skateboarders. Who is the target audience?
questions.explain: The images target young, active people.

questions.q: A public health poster says Wash your hands, save lives. What is its purpose?
hints: It is not selling a brand.
questions.explain: It aims to change behaviour.

reflect.q: What will you look for first next time?

units.parent: Your child analysed how adverts and cartoons use images and words to persuade.
units.teacher: Shows identifying visual elements, target audience, purpose and techniques in adverts and cartoons.
units.done: Ask who a visual text is for, what it wants, and how it persuades.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Essay types
units.topic: Narrative, descriptive, argumentative and reflective essays
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 English Home Language: Writing and Presenting (essays: narrative, descriptive, argumentative, discursive, reflective; planning and paragraphing)
units.intention: Today I am learning the features of different essay types.
units.prompt: Which essay type do you enjoy writing most?

lesson.say: A narrative essay tells a story. A descriptive essay paints a picture with the senses. An argumentative essay takes a side and argues it. A reflective essay explores your own thoughts and growth.
lesson.html: Narrative: story→Descriptive: senses→Argumentative: one side→Reflective: thoughts

lesson.say: Before writing, brainstorm, then make a plan: introduction, three or four body paragraphs, and a conclusion. Each body paragraph has one main idea.
lesson.html:
Brainstorm→Plan→Draft→Edit→Final copy

Most exams give marks for your plan.

lesson.say: Start each paragraph with a topic sentence. Support it with detail or evidence. Link it to the next paragraph with a transition.
lesson.html:
Topic sentence→Support→Link

Vary sentence length to keep the reader interested.

example.q: The topic is The day I learned to stand up for myself. Which essay type fits best?
steps: It is about a personal experience.
It could tell a story and reflect on what you learned.
A narrative or reflective essay fits best.

questions.q: Which essay type takes one side of an issue?
questions.explain: Argumentative essays take one side.

questions.q: Which essay focuses on sights, sounds and smells?
questions.explain: Descriptive essays appeal to the senses.

questions.q: What is a topic sentence?
options: The sentence that states a paragraph's main idea
The last sentence of an essay
hints: It tells what the paragraph is about.
questions.explain: It states the paragraph's main idea.

questions.q: Should school uniforms be scrapped? Which types could fit this topic?
questions.explain: A debate topic suits argumentative or discursive writing.

questions.q: Put the writing process in order.
questions.explain: Brainstorm, plan, draft, edit, final copy.

reflect.q: Which part of essay writing will you work on?

units.parent: Your child learned the features of narrative, descriptive, argumentative and reflective essays.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing essay types, the writing process and paragraph structure.
units.done: Choose the right essay type, plan first, and build strong paragraphs.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Cell division: mitosis
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Life Sciences, Term 1: Cell division (the cell cycle; mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase; importance of mitosis; cancer)
units.intention: Today I am learning how cells divide by mitosis.
units.prompt: Why must the new cells be identical to the parent cell?

lesson.say: Most of a cell's life is spent in interphase, growing and copying its DNA. Then it divides by mitosis, making two identical daughter cells.
lesson.html:
Interphase→Mitosis→Cytokinesis

DNA is copied during interphase.

lesson.say: In prophase, chromosomes become visible. In metaphase, they line up in the middle. In anaphase, the chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles. In telophase, two new nuclei form.
lesson.html:
Prophase→Metaphase→Anaphase→Telophase

Remember PMAT.

lesson.say: Mitosis allows growth, repair of damaged tissue and asexual reproduction. When cell division goes out of control, a tumour can form. This is how cancer develops.
lesson.html:
Growth→Repair→Asexual reproduction

Uncontrolled mitosis can lead to cancer.

example.q: In which phase do chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell?
steps: Think: M for middle.
Metaphase.
The chromosomes line up on the equator of the cell.

questions.q: Put the phases of mitosis in order.
questions.explain: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

questions.q: When is DNA copied?
questions.explain: DNA replicates during interphase.

questions.q: In which phase are chromatids pulled to opposite poles?
questions.explain: Chromatids separate in anaphase.

questions.q: How many daughter cells does mitosis produce?
questions.explain: Two genetically identical daughter cells.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of mitosis?
hints: Sex cells need half the chromosomes.
questions.explain: Sex cells are made by meiosis, not mitosis.

options: Linking it to growth and repair

units.parent: Your child learned the cell cycle and the four phases of mitosis.
units.teacher: Shows sequencing the cell cycle and phases of mitosis, and explaining the role of mitosis and its link to cancer.
units.done: Mitosis makes two identical cells for growth and repair.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Energy flow in ecosystems
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Life Sciences, Term 4: Biosphere to ecosystems (biotic and abiotic factors; trophic levels; food chains and webs; energy pyramids; nutrient cycles)
units.intention: Today I am tracing how energy moves through an ecosystem.
units.prompt: Why are there usually fewer top predators than plants?

lesson.say: An ecosystem has biotic, living factors like plants and animals, and abiotic, non-living factors like sunlight, water, soil and temperature.
lesson.html:
Biotic: living→Abiotic: non-living

Both affect what can live there.

lesson.say: Producers make food from sunlight. Primary consumers eat producers. Secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Decomposers break down dead matter.
lesson.html:
Grass→Springbok→Cheetah

Each step is a trophic level.

lesson.say: Only about ten percent of energy passes to the next level. The rest is used for life processes or lost as heat. That is why energy pyramids get narrower at the top.
lesson.html:
10 000 J→1 000 J→100 J→10 J

Fewer top predators can be supported.

example.q: Grass has 20 000 J of energy. About how much reaches a cheetah that eats a springbok?
steps: Grass to springbok: 10% of 20 000 = 2 000 J.
Springbok to cheetah: 10% of 2 000 = 200 J.
About 200 J.

questions.q: Which is an abiotic factor?
questions.explain: Rainfall is non-living, so abiotic.

questions.q: What is the role of decomposers?
options: Break down dead matter and recycle nutrients
questions.explain: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead matter.

questions.q: In grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, what is the frog?
questions.explain: The frog is a secondary consumer.

questions.q: A producer level has 50 000 J. Using the 10% rule, how much reaches the primary consumers?
Why is energy lost between trophic levels?
options: Used for life processes and lost as heat
questions.explain: Most energy is used or lost as heat.

units.parent: Your child traced how energy flows through ecosystems.
units.teacher: Shows identifying biotic and abiotic factors, trophic levels and applying the 10% energy transfer rule.
units.done: Energy flows from producers to consumers, and about 90% is lost at each step.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Transport in plants
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Life Sciences, Term 3: Support and transport systems in plants (xylem and phloem; transpiration; factors affecting transpiration; wilting)
units.intention: Today I am learning how water and food move through a plant.
units.prompt: Why might a plant wilt on a hot, windy day?

lesson.say: Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots. Phloem carries food, made in the leaves, to all parts of the plant.
lesson.html:
Xylem: water up→Phloem: food everywhere

Together they form vascular bundles.

lesson.say: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves through tiny pores called stomata. It pulls water up the xylem like drinking through a straw.
lesson.html:
🍃 💧

The transpiration pull moves water upwards.

lesson.say: Transpiration is faster when it is hot, windy, bright and dry. It is slower when it is cool, still and humid.
lesson.html:
↑ temperature→↑ wind→↑ light→↓ humidity

If plants lose water faster than they take it in, they wilt.

example.q: Why do plants in the desert often have small, waxy leaves?
steps: Deserts are hot and dry, so transpiration is fast.
Small, waxy leaves lose less water.
This helps the plant survive.

questions.q: What does xylem transport?
questions.explain: Xylem carries water and minerals.

questions.q: What does phloem transport?
questions.explain: Phloem carries sugars from the leaves.

questions.q: What are stomata?
questions.explain: Stomata are tiny pores, mainly on the underside of leaves.

questions.q: Which condition slows transpiration?
hints: The air is already full of water vapour.
questions.explain: Humid air slows water loss from leaves.

questions.q: Why does a plant wilt?
options: It loses more water than it takes in
questions.explain: Water loss greater than uptake makes cells floppy.

units.parent: Your child learned how xylem and phloem transport water and food, and what affects transpiration.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing xylem and phloem, explaining transpiration and factors affecting its rate.
units.done: Xylem carries water up, phloem carries food, and leaves lose water by transpiration.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Managing stress
units.topic: Development of the self in society
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Life Orientation: Development of the self in society (strategies to enhance self-awareness and well-being; coping with stress)
units.intention: Today I am learning to recognise stress and use healthy ways to cope.
units.prompt: What is one healthy thing that helps you when you are stressed?

lesson.say: Stress is your body's response to pressure. A little stress can help you focus. Too much, for too long, can affect sleep, mood, concentration and health.
lesson.html:
Pressure→→→Body response

Signs: headaches, poor sleep, irritability, worry.

lesson.say: Healthy ways to cope include exercise, sleep and talking to someone. Break tasks into steps. Breathe slowly, and make time for things you enjoy.
lesson.html:
Move→Sleep→Talk→Plan→Breathe

Try box breathing: in for 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4.

lesson.say: Unhealthy coping, like isolating yourself or using alcohol, makes stress worse over time. If stress feels overwhelming, talk to a trusted adult, a school counsellor or a helpline.
lesson.html:
Trusted adult→Counsellor→Clinic→Helpline

Asking for help is a strength.

example.q: Andile has three assignments due and cannot sleep. What could help?
steps: Recognise the signs: poor sleep and worry.
Make a plan: list tasks, set small daily goals.
Look after himself: exercise, a regular bedtime, and talk to a teacher about deadlines.

questions.q: Which is a sign of too much stress?
questions.explain: Poor sleep is a common sign of stress.

questions.q: Which is a healthy coping strategy?
questions.explain: Exercise reduces stress hormones.

questions.q: Can some stress be useful?
options: Yes, a little can help you focus
questions.explain: Short-term stress can improve focus.

questions.q: Put box breathing in order.
questions.explain: In, hold, out, hold.

questions.q: Stress has felt overwhelming for weeks. What is the best step?
options: Talk to a counsellor or trusted adult
hints: You don't have to handle it alone.
questions.explain: Talking to a counsellor or trusted adult is the best step.

units.parent: Your child learned to recognise stress and practise healthy coping strategies.
units.teacher: Shows identifying signs of stress, distinguishing healthy from unhealthy coping and knowing where to seek help.
units.done: Notice stress early, use healthy strategies, and ask for help when it is too much.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Human rights in action
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Life Orientation: Democracy and human rights (human rights violations; discrimination; campaigns and organisations that protect human rights)
units.intention: Today I am learning how human rights are protected and how to respond to violations.
units.prompt: Which human rights issue do you care about most?

lesson.say: A human rights violation is when someone's rights are denied or abused. Examples are discrimination, gender-based violence, or a child being kept out of school.
lesson.html:
Discrimination→Violence→Exclusion

Violations can happen at home, school, work or online.

lesson.say: In South Africa, the courts protect rights. So do the Chapter 9 institutions. These include the South African Human Rights Commission, the Commission for Gender Equality and the Public Protector.
lesson.html:
Courts→Human Rights Commission→Gender Commission→Public Protector

Anyone can lodge a complaint with the SAHRC.

lesson.say: You can respond in different ways. You can report it, or support the person affected. You can raise awareness with a campaign, or join an organisation that works on the issue.
lesson.html:
Report→Support→Raise awareness→Join

A campaign needs a clear goal, audience and message.

example.q: A learner is refused entry to a school activity because of their religion. What could be done?
steps: This is unfair discrimination, which violates the right to equality.
The learner and family can raise it with the school and governing body.
If not resolved, they can complain to the SAHRC.

questions.q: Which is a human rights violation?
options: Refusing someone a job because of their race
questions.explain: Refusing a job because of race is unfair discrimination.

questions.q: Which institution handles human rights complaints?
questions.explain: The SAHRC handles human rights complaints.

questions.q: What are Chapter 9 institutions?
hints: Named after a chapter of the Constitution.
questions.explain: Chapter 9 institutions support constitutional democracy.

questions.q: What does a campaign need?
options: A clear goal, audience and message
questions.explain: A clear goal, audience and message.

questions.q: You see someone being bullied online for their sexuality. What is a helpful response?
options: Support them and report the posts
questions.explain: Supporting and reporting helps protect their rights.

units.parent: Your child learned about human rights violations and how they are addressed in South Africa.
units.teacher: Shows identifying violations, knowing Chapter 9 institutions and planning responses and campaigns.
units.done: Human rights are protected by law and by people who take action.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Paying for further study
units.caps: CAPS Grade 10 Life Orientation: Careers and career choices (options after school; financial aid, bursaries, scholarships and loans; requirements)
units.intention: Today I am finding out how to pay for study after school.
units.prompt: Which funding option might suit you?

lesson.say: After matric there are many options. You can study at a university, a university of technology, a TVET college or a private college. You can do a learnership, or go into work or business.
lesson.html: University→TVET college→Learnership→Work or business

lesson.say: NSFAS offers bursaries to qualifying students at public universities and TVET colleges, based on household income. Companies, government departments and charities also offer bursaries and scholarships. Loans must be repaid.
lesson.html:
NSFAS→Bursaries→Scholarships→Student loans

Learnerships let you earn while you learn.

lesson.say: Applications often close in the year before you study, sometimes by September or earlier. Keep certified copies of your ID and results ready, and check the official websites.
lesson.html:
Research→Gather documents→Apply early→Follow up

Beware of scams: you should never pay to apply for NSFAS.

example.q: Thandeka wants to study nursing but her family cannot afford fees. What should she do?
steps: Check whether she qualifies for NSFAS.
Look for health bursaries from provincial health departments and hospital groups.
Apply early and keep copies of all documents.

questions.q: What does NSFAS provide?
questions.explain: NSFAS funds qualifying students at public institutions.

questions.q: What is the difference between a bursary and a loan?
options: A loan must be paid back
A bursary must be paid back with interest
questions.explain: Loans must be repaid. Bursaries usually do not, though some require work-back.

questions.q: What is a learnership?
options: Earning while you learn in a workplace
questions.explain: A learnership combines workplace learning and study.

questions.q: Someone asks you to pay R500 to apply for NSFAS. What is it?
questions.explain: NSFAS applications are free, so this is likely a scam.

questions.q: When should you start researching funding?
questions.explain: Start early, because many deadlines fall in the year before study.

units.parent: Your child learned about study options after school and ways to fund them, including NSFAS, bursaries and learnerships.
units.teacher: Shows knowledge of post-school pathways, funding options, application timing and avoiding scams.
units.done: Research funding early: NSFAS, bursaries, scholarships and learnerships.

units.subject: English
units.title: Explicit and implicit meaning
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Reading (explicit and implicit meanings and attitudes)
units.intention: Today I am finding what a text says directly and what it suggests.
units.prompt: How can you tell how someone feels without them saying it?
units.passage:
The Storm (a 2to.iQ passage)

By four o'clock the sky over the township had turned the colour of a bruise. Mama Dlamini stopped sweeping and stood very still, the broom held like a spear. Somewhere a dog began to bark, then thought better of it.

The first drops were fat and slow, each one landing on the dust with a soft cough. Then the wind arrived, slamming doors that nobody had left open, and the rain came all at once, as if someone had tipped the sky over.

Lindiwe ran for the washing line. She was laughing, though she could not have said why. Her mother's voice followed her, sharp and worried, but the thunder swallowed it whole.

lesson.say: Read the passage, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
The Storm (a 2to.iQ passage)

By four o'clock the sky over the township had turned the colour of a bruise. Mama Dlamini stopped sweeping and stood very still, the broom held like a spear. Somewhere a dog began to bark, then thought better of it.

The first drops were fat and slow, each one landing on the dust with a soft cough. Then the wind arrived, slamming doors that nobody had left open, and the rain came all at once, as if someone had tipped the sky over.

Lindiwe ran for the washing line. She was laughing, though she could not have said why. Her mother's voice followed her, sharp and worried, but the thunder swallowed it whole.

lesson.say: Explicit information is stated directly in the text. The passage tells us plainly that Lindiwe ran for the washing line.
lesson.html: Explicit: stated. Find it and quote it.

lesson.say: Implicit meaning is suggested, not stated. Mama Dlamini holds the broom like a spear, which suggests she is tense and ready, as if facing an enemy.
lesson.html: Implicit: inferred from clues. Explain the clue.

example.q: What does 'her mother's voice followed her, sharp and worried' suggest?
steps: Sharp suggests a raised, urgent tone.
Worried tells us how the mother feels.
Implicitly, the mother thinks Lindiwe may be in danger in the storm.

questions.q: At what time had the sky changed colour?
questions.explain: The first sentence says 'By four o'clock'.

questions.q: What is Mama Dlamini doing when the passage begins?
questions.explain: She 'stopped sweeping'.

questions.q: Why does the writer say the dog 'thought better of it'?
options: To suggest that even the dog sensed something frightening
To show the dog was clever
hints: The dog starts barking, then stops.
Why might an animal go quiet?
questions.explain: It suggests a tense, threatening atmosphere that even the dog feels.

questions.q: What does Lindiwe's laughter suggest about her?
options: She is angry with her mother
hints: She laughs while running in the rain.
questions.explain: Unlike her mother, she finds the storm thrilling.

questions.q: Which of these is implicit rather than explicit?
options: Mama Dlamini is uneasy about the storm
Lindiwe ran for the washing line
The first drops were fat and slow
hints: Which one is never stated directly?
Three are written in the passage.
Her unease is suggested by the spear image.
questions.explain: Her unease is inferred; the others are stated.

units.parent: Your child found what a story states directly and what it suggests.
units.teacher: Shows retrieving explicit information and inferring implicit meanings and attitudes, with reference to the text.
units.done: Explicit: stated. Implicit: suggested by clues you can explain.

units.subject: English
units.title: Writer's effects
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Reading (how writers achieve effects and influence readers)
units.intention: Today I am explaining how a writer's words create effects.
units.prompt: Which words in a story have ever given you goosebumps?
units.passage:
The Storm (a 2to.iQ passage)

By four o'clock the sky over the township had turned the colour of a bruise. Mama Dlamini stopped sweeping and stood very still, the broom held like a spear. Somewhere a dog began to bark, then thought better of it.

The first drops were fat and slow, each one landing on the dust with a soft cough. Then the wind arrived, slamming doors that nobody had left open, and the rain came all at once, as if someone had tipped the sky over.

Lindiwe ran for the washing line. She was laughing, though she could not have said why. Her mother's voice followed her, sharp and worried, but the thunder swallowed it whole.

lesson.say: Read the passage, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
The Storm (a 2to.iQ passage)

By four o'clock the sky over the township had turned the colour of a bruise. Mama Dlamini stopped sweeping and stood very still, the broom held like a spear. Somewhere a dog began to bark, then thought better of it.

The first drops were fat and slow, each one landing on the dust with a soft cough. Then the wind arrived, slamming doors that nobody had left open, and the rain came all at once, as if someone had tipped the sky over.

Lindiwe ran for the washing line. She was laughing, though she could not have said why. Her mother's voice followed her, sharp and worried, but the thunder swallowed it whole.

lesson.say: Writers choose images to make us see and feel. The sky the colour of a bruise suggests something dark, painful and threatening.
lesson.html: colour of a bruise→dark, painful→threat

lesson.say: To explain an effect, first quote the words. Say what they literally mean. Then say what they suggest, and how they make the reader feel.
lesson.html: Quote→Literal meaning→Suggestion→Effect on the reader

example.q: Explain the effect of 'as if someone had tipped the sky over'.
steps: Literally, a huge amount of rain fell suddenly.
Tipping a container suggests all the water pouring out at once.
It makes the storm feel sudden and overwhelming.

questions.q: 'Each one landing on the dust with a soft cough.' What technique is this?
hints: A human action is given to a thing.
questions.explain: Coughing is a human action given to the raindrops.

questions.q: What does 'slamming doors that nobody had left open' suggest about the wind?
options: It is so strong it seems to force its way in
questions.explain: The wind seems powerful enough to force closed doors.

questions.q: What effect does 'the thunder swallowed it whole' create?
options: The thunder is so loud the mother can't be heard
questions.explain: The thunder drowns out her voice completely.

questions.q: What is the best first step when explaining a writer's effect?
options: Give your opinion of the weather
questions.explain: Start by quoting the exact words you will analyse.

questions.q: Why might the writer compare the broom to a spear?
options: To show Mama Dlamini is ready to face the storm like a warrior
To describe the colour of the broom
hints: What is a spear used for?
questions.explain: It presents her as a warrior bracing for the storm.

units.parent: Your child explained how a writer's word choices create atmosphere and feeling.
units.teacher: Shows analysing imagery and figurative language, explaining literal and connotative meanings and their effect on the reader.
units.done: Quote, explain the literal meaning, then what it suggests and how it makes you feel.

units.subject: English
units.title: Summary writing
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Reading and writing (selecting relevant information and summarising it in your own words)
units.intention: Today I am selecting the main points and summarising them.
units.prompt: How would you tell a friend about a film in three sentences?
units.passage:
Saving water at school (a 2to.iQ article)

Last year our school used more water than any other in the district. Some of this was bad luck: a pipe burst under the netball court and went unnoticed for weeks. But much of it was habit. Taps were left running during break, and the gardens were watered at midday, when most of the water simply evaporated.

This year the Grade 10s took charge. They fitted cheap push-taps in the bathrooms, so a tap turns itself off after a few seconds. They moved garden watering to early morning. They also put up a chart outside the office showing the meter reading every Friday, which turned saving water into a competition between classes.

The result surprised everyone. In one term, water use fell by almost a third, and the money saved paid for new library books.

lesson.say: Read the passage, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Saving water at school (a 2to.iQ article)

Last year our school used more water than any other in the district. Some of this was bad luck: a pipe burst under the netball court and went unnoticed for weeks. But much of it was habit. Taps were left running during break, and the gardens were watered at midday, when most of the water simply evaporated.

This year the Grade 10s took charge. They fitted cheap push-taps in the bathrooms, so a tap turns itself off after a few seconds. They moved garden watering to early morning. They also put up a chart outside the office showing the meter reading every Friday, which turned saving water into a competition between classes.

The result surprised everyone. In one term, water use fell by almost a third, and the money saved paid for new library books.

lesson.say: A summary only includes points that answer the question. For example, the question asks how the school saved water. So leave out the burst pipe, because it explains the problem, not the solution.
lesson.html: Read the question→Mark relevant points→Leave out extras

lesson.say: Write the points in your own words, in a smooth paragraph, within the word limit. Don't add your own opinion.
lesson.html: Self-closing taps, early-morning watering, a weekly class competition.

example.q: Summarise how the Grade 10s saved water, in one sentence.
steps: Point 1: taps that switch off by themselves.
Point 2: watering early, so less evaporates. Point 3: a weekly chart that made it a competition.
They fitted self-closing taps, watered the gardens early and made saving water a class competition with a weekly meter chart.

questions.q: The question asks how the school saved water. Which point belongs in the summary?
options: Push-taps were fitted in the bathrooms
A pipe burst under the netball court
The school used the most water in the district
hints: Which one is something they did to save water?
questions.explain: Push-taps are a way of saving water; the others are background or results.

questions.q: Why was watering at midday wasteful?
hints: It is in the first paragraph.
What happens to water in the midday heat?
questions.explain: Most of the water evaporated.

questions.q: Which point should be left out of a summary of the solutions?
hints: Which one is not a solution?
It is part of the problem.
questions.explain: The burst pipe is part of the problem, not the solution.

questions.q: Which version is in your own words and concise?
options: Watering moved to early morning to reduce evaporation.
They moved garden watering to early morning.
The gardens, which had previously been watered at midday when the water evaporated, were now watered in the morning instead.
hints: One is too long, one is opinion.
Short and in your own words.
questions.explain: It is brief, accurate and not copied.

questions.q: What should a summary NOT include?
questions.explain: A summary reports the writer's points, not your views.

units.parent: Your child picked out the main points of an article and summarised them concisely.
units.teacher: Shows selecting relevant information for a specific focus and summarising concisely in own words.
units.done: Answer the question, keep only relevant points, use your own words and no opinions.

units.subject: English
units.title: Directed writing: a persuasive letter
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Directed writing (using and developing ideas from reading; writing for a specific purpose, audience and register)
units.intention: Today I am writing to persuade, using ideas from a text.
units.prompt: What would you ask your principal to change?

lesson.say: Before you write, ask: why am I writing, who will read it, and how formal should I be? A letter to a principal needs a polite, formal register.
lesson.html: Purpose→Audience→Register

lesson.say: Directed writing asks you to use ideas from a passage. Select the ideas, then develop them with your own reasons and examples, rather than copying.
lesson.html: Use the ideas; don't copy the sentences.

lesson.say: To persuade, start with a clear opening. Give your reasons in a logical order, with evidence. Answer objections politely, and end with a confident call to action.
lesson.html: Clear aim→Reasons and evidence→Answer objections→Call to action

example.q: Write an opening sentence for a letter to your principal asking for push-taps.
steps: Purpose: to persuade. Audience: the principal. Register: formal.
State the request politely and clearly.
'I am writing to ask whether the school could install push-taps. This simple change would save water and money.'

questions.q: Which greeting suits a formal letter to a principal?
questions.explain: 'Dear Mr Naidoo,' is polite and formal.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a persuasive letter?
options: To convince the reader to agree or act
questions.explain: Persuasive writing aims to convince.

questions.q: Which is the best way to answer an objection?
options: 'Some may worry about the cost, but push-taps are cheap and soon pay for themselves.'
questions.explain: It respects the concern, then answers it with a reason.

questions.q: Which ending is a clear call to action?
options: 'Could we discuss this at the next staff meeting?'
hints: What should the reader do next?
questions.explain: It asks for a specific next step.

questions.q: When using ideas from a reading passage, you should…
options: develop them in your own words
questions.explain: Select ideas and develop them in your own words.

units.parent: Your child planned a formal persuasive letter using ideas from an article.
units.teacher: Shows adapting register for purpose and audience, developing ideas from reading, and using persuasive structure.
units.done: Know your purpose and reader, develop the ideas, answer objections, end with a request.

units.subject: English
units.title: Descriptive writing
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Composition (descriptive writing: vocabulary, imagery, structure and atmosphere)
units.intention: Today I am writing description that creates a vivid picture.
units.prompt: What place do you know so well you could describe it with your eyes closed?

lesson.say: Description creates a picture in the reader's mind. Instead of saying the market was busy, show it: hawkers calling, the smell of roasting mielies, people squeezing past.
lesson.html:
Tell: The market was busy.

Show: Hawkers sang their prices over the hiss of the grills.

lesson.say: Use more than sight. Sounds, smells, textures and even tastes make a place feel real.
lesson.html: See→Hear→Smell→Touch→Taste

lesson.say: Description still needs a structure. You might move through space, from the gate to the centre. You might move through time, from dawn to dusk. Or you might zoom from a wide view to a small detail.
lesson.html: Wide view→Closer→One small detail

example.q: Improve: 'It was a hot day.'
steps: Choose a sense: touch.
Show the effect of the heat instead of naming it.
'The tar softened under my shoes, and even the shade felt like breath on my neck.'

questions.q: Which sentence shows rather than tells?
options: Steam curled from the pot as the spoon knocked against its sides.
hints: Which one lets you see and hear it?
questions.explain: Specific sights and sounds let the reader experience the scene.

questions.q: Which sense does 'the sour tang of overripe mangoes' appeal to?
hints: You can smell or taste these.
questions.explain: Sour and tang appeal to smell and taste.

questions.q: Which is a good structure for a descriptive piece?
options: Zooming from a wide view to a small detail
questions.explain: Zooming in guides the reader like a camera.

questions.q: Why should description avoid long strings of adjectives?
options: It can feel cluttered; precise verbs and nouns often work better
hints: 'The big, old, tall, grey, sad tree'…
questions.explain: One precise verb or noun often beats several adjectives.

questions.q: What is the main aim of descriptive writing?
options: To create a vivid picture and atmosphere
questions.explain: Description creates a picture and a mood.

units.parent: Your child practised descriptive writing using the senses and a clear structure.
units.teacher: Shows using precise vocabulary, sensory imagery and deliberate structure to create atmosphere.
units.done: Show with the senses, choose precise words, and give the description a shape.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Standard form
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580): Number (standard form; calculating with numbers in standard form)
units.intention: Today I am writing very large and very small numbers in standard form.
units.prompt: Where might you meet a very large or very small number?

lesson.say: Standard form writes a number as a number from 1 up to, but not including, 10, multiplied by a power of 10. 4 500 000 is 4.5 times 10 to the power 6.
lesson.html:
4 500 000→4.5 × 10⁶

The first part must be at least 1 and less than 10.

lesson.say: For numbers less than 1, the power of 10 is negative. 0.00032 is 3.2 times 10 to the power minus 4.
lesson.html: 0.00032→3.2 × 10⁻⁴

lesson.say: To multiply, multiply the first parts and add the powers. Then check the answer is still in standard form.

example.q: Write 0.000067 in standard form.
steps: Move the decimal point to get 6.7.
It moved 5 places.

questions.q: Write 72 000 in standard form.
hints: The first part must be between 1 and 10.

questions.q: Write 0.0059 in standard form.
hints: It is less than 1, so the power is negative.

questions.q: Write 3.4 × 10³ as an ordinary number.
Which number is NOT in standard form?
hints: Is it from 1 to less than 10?
questions.explain: 12 is not less than 10, so 12 × 10⁴ should be 1.2 × 10⁵.

options: Checking the first part is between 1 and 10

units.parent: Your child wrote very large and very small numbers in standard form, and calculated with them.
units.teacher: Shows converting to and from standard form, including negative powers, and multiplying in standard form.
units.done: Standard form: a number from 1 to less than 10, times a power of 10.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Simultaneous equations
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580): Algebra and graphs (solving simultaneous linear equations by elimination and substitution)
units.intention: Today I am solving two equations with two unknowns.
units.prompt: Where might two facts together tell you two unknown prices?

lesson.say: Simultaneous equations are two equations that are both true at the same time. You need two equations to find two unknowns.
lesson.html: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4

lesson.say: Add or subtract the equations to remove one unknown. Adding x plus y equals 10 to x minus y equals 4 gives 2x equals 14, so x is 7.
lesson.html: Add: 2x = 14→x = 7→y = 3

lesson.say: You can also make one unknown the subject and substitute it into the other equation. Always check your answer in both equations.

example.q: Solve 2x + y = 11 and x + y = 7.
steps: Subtract the second equation from the first: x = 4.
Substitute: 4 + y = 7, so y = 3.

questions.q: Solve x + y = 12 and x − y = 2.
questions.explain: 2x = 14, so x = 7 and y = 5. Check: 7 − 5 = 2 ✓.

questions.q: If 3x + y = 14 and x + y = 6, what is x?
hints: Subtract the second from the first.

questions.q: Using x = 4 and x + y = 6, what is y?
To eliminate y from 2x + 3y = 13 and 4x − 3y = 5, you should…
hints: Look at the y terms: +3y and −3y.
questions.explain: +3y and −3y cancel when you add.

questions.q: Two pens and a ruler cost $5. One pen and a ruler cost $3.50. How much is one pen?
questions.explain: Subtracting gives p = $1.50.

options: Choosing whether to add or subtract

units.parent: Your child solved pairs of equations with two unknowns.
units.teacher: Shows solving simultaneous linear equations by elimination and substitution, and checking solutions.
units.done: Remove one unknown, solve, substitute back, then check.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Straight-line graphs
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580): Coordinate geometry (gradient; y = mx + c; parallel lines)
units.intention: Today I am finding gradients and equations of straight lines.
units.prompt: What does steepness mean on a hill or a graph?

lesson.say: Every straight line, except a vertical one, can be written as y equals m x plus c. Here, m is the gradient, which is how steep the line is. And c is where the line crosses the y-axis.
lesson.html: m: gradient→c: y-intercept

lesson.say: The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x between two points. From 1, 3 to 3, 7, y goes up 4 while x goes up 2, so the gradient is 2.
Parallel lines have the same gradient. A negative gradient means the line goes down from left to right.
lesson.html: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 5 are parallel.

example.q: Find the equation of the line through (0, −1) with gradient 3.
steps: The line crosses the y-axis at −1, so c = −1.
The gradient is 3, so m = 3.

questions.q: What is the gradient of y = 5x − 2?
hints: m is the number in front of x.

questions.q: Where does y = 4x + 7 cross the y-axis?
questions.explain: c = 7, so it crosses at (0, 7).

questions.q: Find the gradient of the line through (2, 1) and (4, 9).
Which line is parallel to y = 3x + 2?
hints: Parallel lines have the same gradient.
questions.explain: y = 3x − 4 also has gradient 3.

questions.q: A line has a negative gradient. What does it look like?
options: It goes down from left to right
It goes up from left to right
hints: Negative: y falls as x grows.
questions.explain: A negative gradient slopes down from left to right.

options: Reading m and c from the equation
Change in y over change in x

units.parent: Your child found the gradient and equation of straight lines.
units.teacher: Shows calculating gradient from two points, interpreting y = mx + c, and identifying parallel lines.
units.done: y = mx + c: m is the gradient, c is the y-intercept.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Angles in polygons
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580): Geometry (angle properties of polygons; interior and exterior angles of regular polygons)
units.intention: Today I am working out the angles in polygons.
units.prompt: Why do you think bees build hexagons?

lesson.say: The interior angles of a polygon with n sides add up to n minus 2, times 180 degrees. A pentagon has 5 sides, so its angles add up to 540 degrees.
lesson.html: Sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°

lesson.say: The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360 degrees. In a regular polygon they are all equal, so each one is 360 divided by the number of sides.
lesson.html: Exterior angles add to 360°→Regular: 360° ÷ n

lesson.say: At each corner, the interior and exterior angles lie on a straight line, so they add up to 180 degrees.
lesson.html: interior + exterior = 180°

example.q: Find each interior angle of a regular hexagon.
steps: Each exterior angle: 360° ÷ 6 = 60°.

questions.q: What do the interior angles of a quadrilateral add up to, in degrees?
What do the interior angles of a pentagon add up to, in degrees?
Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. How many sides does it have?
Find each interior angle of a regular octagon, in degrees.
What do the exterior angles of a 20-sided polygon add up to?
hints: Does the number of sides matter for exterior angles?
questions.explain: The exterior angles of any polygon add to 360°.

units.parent: Your child worked out interior and exterior angles of polygons.
units.teacher: Shows using the interior angle sum and exterior angle properties of polygons, including regular polygons.
units.done: Interior sum: (n − 2) × 180°. Exterior sum: always 360°.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Averages from frequency tables
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580): Statistics (mean, median and mode from frequency tables; estimating the mean from grouped data)
units.intention: Today I am finding averages from frequency tables.
units.prompt: Why might a sports coach keep a frequency table?

lesson.say: A frequency table shows how many times each value occurs, for example the number of goals scored in 10 matches.
lesson.html:
Goals: 0, 1, 2, 3

Frequency: 2, 4, 3, 1

lesson.say: To find the mean, multiply each value by its frequency, add these up, then divide by the total frequency.
When data is grouped, for example heights from 150 to 160 centimetres, you don't know the exact values. Use the midpoint of each group to estimate the mean.
lesson.html:
150 to 160 cm→midpoint 155

The answer is an estimate.

example.q: Values 1, 2, 3 have frequencies 5, 3, 2. Find the mean.
steps: Total frequency: 5 + 3 + 2 = 10.

questions.q: Goals 0, 1, 2, 3 have frequencies 2, 4, 3, 1. What is the mode?
hints: The mode is the value with the highest frequency.
questions.explain: 1 goal happened most often (4 times).

questions.q: Goals 0, 1, 2, 3 have frequencies 2, 4, 3, 1. How many matches were there?
Values 2, 4, 6 have frequencies 1, 2, 1. Find the mean.
What is the midpoint of the group 20 to 30?
Why is a mean from grouped data only an estimate?
options: We don't know the exact values in each group
hints: What do we use instead of the real values?
questions.explain: We use midpoints because the exact values are unknown.

units.parent: Your child found averages from frequency tables, including grouped data.
units.teacher: Shows calculating mean, median and mode from frequency tables and estimating the mean from grouped data.
units.done: Mean from a table: add up value × frequency, then divide by the total frequency.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: Cells, diffusion and osmosis
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Biology (plant and animal cells; diffusion; osmosis)
units.intention: Today I am learning how substances move into and out of cells.
units.prompt: Why do you think wilted lettuce goes crisp in cold water?

lesson.say: Animal and plant cells both have a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane. Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
lesson.html: Both: nucleus, cytoplasm, membrane→Plants also: wall, chloroplasts, vacuole

lesson.say: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. This is called moving down a concentration gradient. It is how oxygen gets into cells.
lesson.html: Higher concentration→Lower concentration

lesson.say: Osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one. Plant cells take in water by osmosis and become firm.
lesson.html: Water moves towards the more concentrated solution.

example.q: Why does a slice of potato in very salty water go soft?
steps: The salty water is more concentrated than the potato cells.
Water leaves the cells by osmosis.
The cells lose water and become soft (flaccid).

questions.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but not animal cells?
hints: Which gives plants a rigid shape?
questions.explain: Only plant cells have a cell wall.

questions.q: What is the function of chloroplasts?
questions.explain: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

questions.q: In diffusion, particles move…
questions.explain: Diffusion is from higher to lower concentration.

questions.q: Osmosis is the movement of…
options: water through a partially permeable membrane
hints: It is a special kind of diffusion.
questions.explain: Osmosis is water moving through a partially permeable membrane.

questions.q: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens?
options: It takes in water and becomes firm
hints: Pure water is more dilute than the cell.
questions.explain: Water enters by osmosis; the cell wall keeps it from bursting, so it becomes firm.

options: Comparing the two kinds of cell

units.parent: Your child learnt how cells are built and how water and other substances move in and out.
units.teacher: Shows comparing plant and animal cells, and explaining diffusion and osmosis in terms of concentration.
units.done: Diffusion: higher to lower concentration. Osmosis: water through a membrane.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: States of matter
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Chemistry (states of matter; changes of state; the kinetic particle model; diffusion in gases)
units.intention: Today I am explaining solids, liquids and gases using particles.
units.prompt: Why can you smell food cooking from another room?

lesson.say: In a solid, particles are packed closely in a regular pattern and vibrate. In a liquid they are close but move around each other. In a gas they are far apart and move quickly in all directions.
lesson.html: Solid: fixed, vibrate→Liquid: close, flow→Gas: far apart, fast

lesson.say: Heating gives particles more energy. Melting turns a solid into a liquid; boiling turns a liquid into a gas. Cooling reverses these: condensing and freezing.
lesson.html:
Solid→Liquid→Gas

Melting, then boiling. Back again: condensing, then freezing.

lesson.say: Gases diffuse faster at higher temperatures, because the particles move faster. Lighter gas particles also diffuse faster than heavier ones.
lesson.html: Hotter: faster particles, faster diffusion.

example.q: Explain why a puddle dries up on a sunny day.
steps: The sun heats the water particles.
Some particles at the surface gain enough energy to escape as a gas.
This is evaporation, so the puddle slowly disappears.

questions.q: In which state are particles arranged in a regular pattern?
questions.explain: Solids have a regular, fixed arrangement.

questions.q: What is the change from gas to liquid called?
hints: Think of a cold window in a steamy kitchen.
questions.explain: Gas to liquid is condensation.

questions.q: Why can gases be compressed easily?
options: There are large spaces between the particles
hints: So they can be pushed together.
questions.explain: The large gaps between particles can be squeezed.

questions.q: What happens to the particles when a solid is heated?
questions.explain: The particles gain energy and vibrate more.

questions.q: Which gas diffuses fastest at the same temperature?
options: The one with the lightest particles
The one with the heaviest particles
questions.explain: Lighter particles move faster, so they diffuse faster.

units.parent: Your child explained solids, liquids and gases, and changes of state, using particles.
units.teacher: Shows using the kinetic particle model to explain states, changes of state and rates of diffusion.
units.done: More energy, faster particles: solids melt, liquids boil and gases spread faster.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: Atoms and the periodic table
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Chemistry (atomic structure; proton number and mass number; groups in the periodic table)
units.intention: Today I am finding what is inside an atom.
units.prompt: What do you think everything is made of?

lesson.say: An atom has a tiny nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells around it. Protons are positive, electrons are negative, and neutrons have no charge.
lesson.html: Proton: +1→Neutron: 0→Electron: −1

lesson.say: The proton number is the number of protons. The mass number is protons plus neutrons. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
lesson.html: Sodium: proton number 11, mass number 23, so 12 neutrons.

lesson.say: Elements are arranged in order of proton number. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways.
lesson.html: Group I metals all have 1 outer electron.

example.q: Carbon has proton number 6 and mass number 12. How many protons, neutrons and electrons?
steps: Protons = proton number = 6.
Neutrons = 12 − 6 = 6.
Electrons = protons = 6 in a neutral atom.

questions.q: Which particle has a negative charge?
questions.explain: Electrons are negative.

questions.q: An atom has proton number 8 and mass number 16. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explain: 16 − 8 = 8 neutrons.

questions.q: Chlorine has proton number 17. How many electrons does a chlorine atom have?
questions.explain: Electrons = protons = 17.

questions.q: Why do elements in the same group react in similar ways?
options: They have the same number of outer electrons
They have the same number of neutrons
questions.explain: Same number of outer electrons, so similar reactions.

questions.q: Where are protons and neutrons found?
questions.explain: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.

units.parent: Your child learnt what atoms are made of and how the periodic table is organised.
units.teacher: Shows describing atomic structure, calculating subatomic particles, and relating group number to outer electrons.
units.done: Protons give the proton number; add neutrons for the mass number.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: Speed and motion graphs
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Physics (speed; distance–time and speed–time graphs; acceleration)
units.intention: Today I am reading motion graphs and working out speed and acceleration.
units.prompt: How would you show a taxi trip on a graph?

lesson.say: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. A cyclist who travels 30 metres in 6 seconds has an average speed of 5 metres per second.
lesson.html: speed = distance ÷ time

lesson.say: On a distance–time graph, the gradient is the speed. A straight sloping line means constant speed; a flat line means the object is not moving.
lesson.html: Steeper: faster→Flat: stopped

lesson.say: On a speed–time graph, the gradient is the acceleration, and the area under the line is the distance travelled.
lesson.html: Gradient: acceleration→Area: distance

example.q: A car speeds up from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s. Find its acceleration.
steps: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time.
= 5 m/s².

questions.q: A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. What is her average speed, in m/s?
On a distance–time graph, what does a horizontal line show?
questions.explain: No change in distance means it is not moving.

questions.q: On a speed–time graph, what does the gradient show?
questions.explain: The gradient of speed against time is acceleration.

questions.q: A bus slows from 15 m/s to 5 m/s in 5 s. What is its deceleration, in m/s²?
An object moves at a steady 10 m/s for 6 s. Using the area under a speed–time graph, how far does it go, in metres?

units.parent: Your child worked out speed and acceleration, and read motion graphs.
units.teacher: Shows calculating speed and acceleration, and interpreting gradients and areas on motion graphs.
units.done: Distance–time: gradient is speed. Speed–time: gradient is acceleration, area is distance.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: Energy resources and efficiency
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Physics (energy stores and transfers; efficiency; energy resources)
units.intention: Today I am tracking energy transfers and working out efficiency.
units.prompt: Where does your home's electricity come from?

lesson.say: Energy is stored in different ways, such as chemical, kinetic, gravitational potential and thermal. Energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred.
lesson.html: Chemical (coal)→Thermal→Kinetic (turbine)→Electrical

lesson.say: Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input. No machine is 100 percent efficient: some energy is always wasted, often as heat.
lesson.html: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100%

lesson.say: Coal, oil and gas are non-renewable and release carbon dioxide. Solar, wind and hydroelectric power are renewable, but they can depend on the weather or the place.
lesson.html: Non-renewable: coal, gas, oil→Renewable: solar, wind, hydro

example.q: A bulb takes in 200 J of electrical energy and gives out 40 J of light. Find its efficiency.
steps: Useful output = 40 J; total input = 200 J.

questions.q: A motor takes in 500 J and gives 400 J of useful kinetic energy. What is its efficiency, as a percentage? (Type the number only.)
Which is a renewable energy resource?
questions.explain: Wind won't run out; the others are fossil fuels.

questions.q: What usually happens to wasted energy?
options: It is transferred to the surroundings as heat
questions.explain: Wasted energy usually spreads out as heat.

questions.q: What is one disadvantage of solar power?
options: It doesn't produce electricity at night
questions.explain: Solar panels need light, so they don't work at night.

questions.q: In a coal power station, what is the first energy store?
hints: Energy is stored in the coal.
questions.explain: Coal stores chemical energy.

units.parent: Your child followed energy transfers, worked out efficiency and compared energy resources.
units.teacher: Shows describing energy stores and transfers, calculating efficiency, and evaluating renewable and non-renewable resources.
units.done: Energy is transferred, never destroyed. Efficiency = useful ÷ total.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Exponential growth and decay
units.caps: IB MYP Mathematics, year 5 (extended): Algebra (exponential functions as models of growth and decay). Key concept: Change. Global context: Globalization and sustainability.
units.intention: Today I am modelling growth and decay with exponential functions.
units.prompt: Why do savings grow faster the longer you leave them?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Exponential models describe change that speeds up or slows down. Examples are population growth and how medicines leave the body. Key concept: Change. Global context: Globalization and sustainability.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Exponential models describe change that speeds up or slows down. Examples are population growth and how medicines leave the body.

Key concept: Change · Global context: Globalization and sustainability
