lesson.say: When something grows by the same percentage each period, multiply by the same factor each time. Growing 10 percent a year means multiplying by 1.1.
lesson.html: y = a × bⁿ, with b = 1.1 for 10% growth

lesson.say: When something decreases by a percentage, the factor is less than 1. Losing 20 percent each hour means multiplying by 0.8.
lesson.html: Decay: b = 1 − rate, for example 0.8

lesson.say: Linear change adds the same amount each time. Exponential change multiplies by the same factor each time, so it eventually grows much faster.
lesson.html: Linear: + the same amount→Exponential: × the same factor

example.q: A town of 10 000 people grows by 5% a year. Estimate its population after 2 years.
steps: Factor = 1.05.
= 11 025 people.

questions.q: What factor represents 10% growth per year?
What factor represents 20% decay per hour?
A 400 mg dose of medicine halves every 6 hours. How much is left after 12 hours, in mg?
$1 000 grows by 10% a year. How much is there after 2 years, in dollars?
Which sequence shows exponential growth?
questions.explain: Each term is multiplied by 2.

units.parent: Your child modelled things that grow or shrink by a percentage, such as savings and medicine doses.
units.teacher: Criteria A and D: models growth and decay with exponential functions, distinguishes linear from exponential change and applies models in context.
units.done: Exponential: multiply by the same factor. Above 1 grows, below 1 decays.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Measuring heights with trigonometry
units.caps: IB MYP Mathematics, year 5: Geometry and trigonometry (right-angled trigonometry; angles of elevation). Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Orientation in space and time.
units.intention: Today I am using trigonometry to measure heights I can't reach.
units.prompt: How could you find the height of your school without climbing it?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Relationships between angles and lengths let us measure what we cannot reach. Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Orientation in space and time.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Relationships between angles and lengths let us measure what we cannot reach.

Key concept: Relationships · Global context: Orientation in space and time

lesson.say: In a right-angled triangle, sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent.
lesson.html: sin = O/H→cos = A/H→tan = O/A

lesson.say: The angle of elevation is the angle you look up from the horizontal. If you know how far you are from a tree and the angle to its top, tangent gives the height.
lesson.html: height = distance × tan(angle)

lesson.say: Your eyes are above the ground, so add your eye height to the answer.
lesson.html: Total height = distance × tan(angle) + eye height

example.q: You stand 20 m from a building. The angle of elevation to the top is 45°, and your eyes are 1.5 m high. Find its height. (tan 45° = 1)
steps: Height above your eyes = 20 × tan 45° = 20 × 1 = 20 m.
Add your eye height: 20 + 1.5.
The building is 21.5 m tall.

questions.q: Which ratio uses the opposite and adjacent sides?
questions.explain: tan = opposite ÷ adjacent.

questions.q: You stand 10 m from a tree. The angle of elevation is 45° (tan 45° = 1). How tall is the tree above your eye level, in metres?
Distance 30 m, angle of elevation with tan = 0.5, eye height 1.6 m. What is the total height, in metres?
What is an angle of elevation?
options: The angle looking up from the horizontal
The angle at the top of the object
questions.explain: It is measured up from the horizontal.

questions.q: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is…
options: the longest side, opposite the right angle
next to the angle you are using
questions.explain: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.

units.parent: Your child used trigonometry to measure heights without climbing.
units.teacher: Criteria A and D: applies right-angled trigonometry and angles of elevation to indirect measurement, including adjusting for eye height.
units.done: height = distance × tan(angle), plus your eye height.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Is it fair? Comparing data
units.caps: IB MYP Mathematics, year 5: Statistics and probability (comparing distributions; sampling and bias). Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Fairness and development.
units.intention: Today I am comparing data sets fairly and checking for bias.
units.prompt: How would you show that something at school is unfair?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Comparing data sets fairly helps communities make decisions about fairness and development. Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Fairness and development.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Comparing data sets fairly helps communities make decisions about fairness and development.

Key concept: Relationships · Global context: Fairness and development

lesson.say: To compare two groups, compare a measure of centre, such as the median. Also compare a measure of spread, such as the interquartile range.
lesson.html: Centre: median or mean→Spread: range or IQR

lesson.say: A sample must represent the population. Asking only people at one shop, or only people online, can bias the results.
lesson.html: Ask: who was left out?

lesson.say: Write conclusions that refer to the data, and say how certain you can be. Small samples give weaker conclusions.
lesson.html: 'Based on this sample, it is likely that…'

example.q: School A's median travel time is 35 minutes (IQR 20). School B's is 20 minutes (IQR 5). Compare them.
steps: School A's learners travel longer: a median of 35 against 20 minutes.
School A's times are much more spread out: an IQR of 20 against 5.
School A's learners travel further, and their journeys vary more.

questions.q: Which pair compares both centre and spread?
questions.explain: The median measures centre; the IQR measures spread.

questions.q: A survey about public transport asks only car owners. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Leaving out transport users biases the results.

questions.q: Group A: median 60, IQR 10. Group B: median 72, IQR 10. How much higher is B's median?
Which conclusion is most appropriate from a sample of 20 learners?
options: 'This sample suggests…, but a larger sample would be more reliable.'
'This proves it for every school in the world.'
questions.explain: A small sample supports a tentative conclusion.

questions.q: Two groups have the same median, but Group A has a much larger IQR. What does this mean?
options: Group A's data is more spread out
questions.explain: A larger IQR means more variation in the middle half.

units.parent: Your child compared sets of data fairly and checked surveys for bias.
units.teacher: Criteria A and D: compares distributions using centre and spread, identifies sampling bias and draws justified, appropriately tentative conclusions.
units.done: Compare centre and spread, check the sample, and say how sure you are.

units.subject: Language and Literature
units.title: Text and context
units.caps: IB MYP Language and Literature, year 5: Criterion A, Analysing (how context shapes the creation and reception of a text). Key concept: Connections. Global context: Orientation in space and time.
units.intention: Today I am exploring how history shapes the meaning of a poem.
units.prompt: What habits have you picked up from your family?
units.passage:
Pass (a 2to.iQ poem, set in 1970s South Africa)

My father kept a small brown book
closer than his wallet, closer than his name.
Each morning he touched his pocket twice,
the way you check a wound.

Today I carry nothing but my phone,
and walk wherever the road allows.
Some mornings I still touch my pocket twice,
and do not know whose habit that is.

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Texts connect to the times and places in which they are written and read. Knowing the context deepens our understanding. Key concept: Connections. Global context: Orientation in space and time.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Texts connect to the times and places in which they are written and read. Knowing the context deepens our understanding.

Key concept: Connections · Global context: Orientation in space and time

lesson.say: Read the text, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Pass (a 2to.iQ poem, set in 1970s South Africa)

My father kept a small brown book
closer than his wallet, closer than his name.
Each morning he touched his pocket twice,
the way you check a wound.

Today I carry nothing but my phone,
and walk wherever the road allows.
Some mornings I still touch my pocket twice,
and do not know whose habit that is.

lesson.say: Context is the time, place and situation of a text. Under apartheid, pass laws forced Black South Africans to carry a pass book. The police could arrest anyone found without one.
lesson.html: The 'small brown book' is a pass book.

lesson.say: The poem connects two times. The father's fear lives on as a habit in the child, who is free to walk wherever the road allows.
lesson.html: Father: pass book, fear→Child: freedom, an inherited habit

example.q: Why does the father touch his pocket 'the way you check a wound'?
steps: You check a wound because it hurts and you worry about it.
The pass book was a constant source of danger and pain.
The simile shows that carrying the pass was a daily injury.

questions.q: What is the 'small brown book'?
hints: The poem is set in the 1970s.
questions.explain: It is the pass book Black South Africans were forced to carry.

questions.q: Why did the father keep it 'closer than his name'?
options: Without it he could be arrested
hints: What happened to people without a pass?
questions.explain: Being found without it could mean arrest.

questions.q: What does the child's habit of touching their pocket suggest?
options: The past still affects the present
The child has lost their phone
questions.explain: The father's fear has been passed down as a habit.

questions.q: Which phrase contrasts most with the father's life?
questions.explain: Freedom of movement contrasts with the pass laws.

questions.q: Why does knowing the context help readers?
options: It explains the book and the fear behind the habit
It tells us the poet's age
hints: Without context, what is the book?
questions.explain: Context reveals what the book is and why it was feared.

units.parent: Your child explored how South African history shapes the meaning of a poem.
units.teacher: Criterion A: analyses how historical and cultural context shapes meaning, and explains connections between past and present in a text.
units.done: Ask when and where a text comes from: context changes what it means.

units.subject: Language and Literature
units.title: Rhetoric: ethos, pathos, logos
units.caps: IB MYP Language and Literature, year 5: Criteria A and D, Analysing and Using language (rhetorical appeals in speeches). Key concept: Communication. Global context: Fairness and development.
units.intention: Today I am analysing how speakers persuade with ethos, pathos and logos.
units.prompt: What would you ask your school to change, and how would you convince them?
units.passage:
From a learner's speech to the school governing body (a 2to.iQ text)

I have been a learner here for nine years, and I have served on the learner council for three. Last winter, 140 of our learners walked more than five kilometres to school, in the dark. One of them was my little sister. She told me she counts her steps so she won't feel afraid. A school bus would cost less per learner than the new sports scoreboard. Surely our learners' safety matters more than our scores.

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Speakers use rhetorical appeals to persuade audiences to act for fairness. Key concept: Communication. Global context: Fairness and development.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Speakers use rhetorical appeals to persuade audiences to act for fairness.

Key concept: Communication · Global context: Fairness and development

lesson.say: Read the text, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
From a learner's speech to the school governing body (a 2to.iQ text)

I have been a learner here for nine years, and I have served on the learner council for three. Last winter, 140 of our learners walked more than five kilometres to school, in the dark. One of them was my little sister. She told me she counts her steps so she won't feel afraid. A school bus would cost less per learner than the new sports scoreboard. Surely our learners' safety matters more than our scores.

lesson.say: Ethos builds trust in the speaker. Pathos appeals to emotion. Logos appeals to logic and evidence.
lesson.html: Ethos: trust→Pathos: emotion→Logos: logic

lesson.say: Strong speeches combine all three. Too much emotion can seem manipulative; too much data can feel cold.
lesson.html: Look for all three working together.

example.q: Which appeal is 'I have served on the learner council for three years'?
steps: It tells us about the speaker.
It shows experience and responsibility.
It builds trust: ethos.

questions.q: 'She counts her steps so she won't feel afraid' is mainly…
hints: How does it make you feel?
It is about fear and a little sister.
questions.explain: It appeals to the audience's emotions.

questions.q: 'A school bus would cost less per learner than the new scoreboard' is mainly…
questions.explain: It uses a logical cost comparison.

questions.q: '140 of our learners walked more than five kilometres' appeals to…
questions.explain: A statistic is logical evidence.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the final sentence?
options: To appeal clearly to the audience's values
questions.explain: It challenges the audience to act on their values.

questions.q: Why might a speech that uses only pathos be weaker?
options: It can seem manipulative without evidence
questions.explain: Without evidence, emotion alone can seem manipulative.

units.parent: Your child analysed how a speaker persuades using trust, emotion and logic.
units.teacher: Criteria A and D: identifies and evaluates rhetorical appeals and their combined effect on an audience.
units.done: Ethos builds trust, pathos moves feelings, logos gives reasons.

units.subject: Language and Literature
units.title: Organising an analytical essay
units.caps: IB MYP Language and Literature, year 5: Criterion B, Organising (structuring an analytical response with a thesis and developed paragraphs). Key concept: Communication. Global context: Personal and cultural expression.
units.intention: Today I am organising an analytical essay.
units.prompt: What makes an essay easy to follow?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Clear organisation helps writers communicate their interpretation persuasively. Key concept: Communication. Global context: Personal and cultural expression.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Clear organisation helps writers communicate their interpretation persuasively.

Key concept: Communication · Global context: Personal and cultural expression

lesson.say: An analytical essay begins with a thesis: your interpretation of the text, which the essay will prove. It should be arguable, not just a fact.
lesson.html:
Fact: The poem is about a pass book.

Thesis: The poem shows how the trauma of the pass laws is inherited by the next generation.

lesson.say: Each paragraph makes a point about the text. It includes a short quotation and analyses the language. Then it links back to the thesis.
lesson.html: Point→Quotation→Analysis→Link

lesson.say: Use transitions to guide the reader, such as furthermore, in contrast and as a result. End with a conclusion that shows why your thesis matters, not just a repeat.
lesson.html: Transitions: furthermore, in contrast, as a result

example.q: Turn 'The father is scared' into an analytical sentence.
steps: Add evidence: he touches his pocket “the way you check a wound”.
Analyse: the simile links the pass book to pain.
“The simile ‘the way you check a wound’ suggests the pass book is a constant injury, not simply a document.”

questions.q: Which is an arguable thesis?
options: The poem shows how fear can outlive the law that caused it.
The poem is about a book.
questions.explain: It is an interpretation that needs proving.

questions.q: What comes after the quotation in an analytical paragraph?
questions.explain: After the quotation, analyse its language.

questions.q: Which transition shows contrast?
questions.explain: 'In contrast' signals a difference.

questions.q: What should a conclusion do?
options: Repeat the introduction word for word
questions.explain: A conclusion shows the significance of the argument.

questions.q: Why embed short quotations rather than long ones?
options: So the analysis focuses on precise words
questions.explain: Short quotations keep the focus on precise language.

units.parent: Your child practised organising an analytical essay with a clear thesis and paragraphs.
units.teacher: Criterion B: organises an analytical response with an arguable thesis, structured paragraphs, embedded evidence and purposeful transitions.
units.done: Arguable thesis, point-quote-analyse-link paragraphs, and a conclusion that matters.

units.subject: Sciences
units.title: Rates of reaction
units.caps: IB MYP Sciences, year 5: Chemistry (factors affecting rate of reaction; collision theory). Key concept: Change. Global context: Scientific and technical innovation.
units.intention: Today I am explaining what makes reactions faster or slower.
units.prompt: Why do we keep food in the fridge?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Understanding what changes the rate of reactions lets engineers make processes faster, safer and cleaner. Key concept: Change. Global context: Scientific and technical innovation.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Understanding what changes the rate of reactions lets engineers make processes faster, safer and cleaner.

Key concept: Change · Global context: Scientific and technical innovation

lesson.say: Particles react when they collide with enough energy. More frequent or more energetic collisions mean a faster reaction.
lesson.html: Faster rate = more successful collisions each second

lesson.say: Increasing temperature, concentration or surface area increases the rate. A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.
lesson.html: Temperature→Concentration→Surface area→Catalyst

lesson.say: Rate can be measured by timing how much gas forms, or how quickly mass is lost.
lesson.html: rate = amount of change ÷ time

example.q: Why does powdered chalk react faster with acid than a lump of chalk?
steps: Powder has a much larger surface area.
More particles are exposed to the acid.
More collisions each second, so a faster reaction.

questions.q: According to collision theory, what must happen for particles to react?
options: They must collide with enough energy
They must be the same colour
questions.explain: Particles must collide with enough energy.

questions.q: What happens to the rate when temperature increases?
questions.explain: Faster particles collide more often and with more energy.

questions.q: What does a catalyst do?
options: Speeds up a reaction without being used up
questions.explain: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up.

questions.q: A reaction produces 60 cm³ of gas in 30 s. What is the average rate, in cm³/s?
Why do kitchens chop vegetables into small pieces to cook them quickly?
options: Smaller pieces have more surface area
questions.explain: Small pieces have more surface area, so heat reaches more of the food.

units.parent: Your child explained what makes chemical reactions faster or slower.
units.teacher: Criteria A and B: explains rate using collision theory, predicts the effect of variables and calculates rate from data.
units.done: More successful collisions each second means a faster reaction.

units.subject: Sciences
units.title: Inheritance
units.caps: IB MYP Sciences, year 5: Biology (genes, alleles, dominant and recessive inheritance; Punnett squares). Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Identities and relationships.
units.intention: Today I am predicting how traits are inherited.
units.prompt: Which of your features came from your family?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: The relationships between genes and the traits they produce help explain both family resemblance and human variety. Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Identities and relationships.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: The relationships between genes and the traits they produce help explain both family resemblance and human variety.

Key concept: Relationships · Global context: Identities and relationships

lesson.say: Genes are sections of DNA that code for traits. Different versions of a gene are called alleles. You inherit one allele from each parent.
lesson.html: DNA→Gene→Allele

lesson.say: A dominant allele shows its effect even with only one copy. A recessive allele shows only if both copies are recessive. We write dominant alleles with a capital letter and recessive ones with a small letter.
lesson.html: Bb: the dominant trait shows · bb: the recessive trait shows

lesson.say: A Punnett square shows the possible combinations from two parents. Two Bb parents give BB, Bb, Bb and bb: a 1 in 4 chance of the recessive trait.
lesson.html: Bb × Bb → BB, Bb, Bb, bb → 3 : 1

example.q: A Bb parent and a bb parent have a child. What is the chance the child shows the recessive trait?
steps: Bb gives B or b; bb gives only b.
Combinations: Bb, Bb, bb, bb.
2 out of 4 are bb: a 50% chance.

questions.q: What is an allele?
questions.explain: An allele is a version of a gene.

questions.q: Which genotype shows the recessive trait?
questions.explain: Only bb shows the recessive trait.

questions.q: How many alleles of each gene do you inherit from each parent?
questions.explain: One from each parent, two in total.

questions.q: Two Bb parents have a child. What is the percentage chance that the child is bb? (Type the number only.)
BB × bb. What genotype will all the children have?
hints: One parent can only give B.
The other can only give b.
questions.explain: Every child gets B from one parent and b from the other.

units.parent: Your child predicted how traits are passed from parents to children.
units.teacher: Criterion A: explains inheritance with genes and alleles, and uses Punnett squares to predict genotypes and probabilities.
units.done: One allele from each parent. Dominant shows with one copy; recessive needs two.

units.subject: Sciences
units.title: Newton's laws of motion
units.caps: IB MYP Sciences, year 5: Physics (forces; Newton's three laws; F = ma). Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Orientation in space and time.
units.intention: Today I am explaining motion with Newton's three laws.
units.prompt: Why do you lurch forward when a taxi brakes?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Relationships between force, mass and motion explain how everything moves, from minibus taxis to rockets. Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Orientation in space and time.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Relationships between force, mass and motion explain how everything moves, from minibus taxis to rockets.

Key concept: Relationships · Global context: Orientation in space and time

lesson.say: An object stays still, or keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line. This changes only when an unbalanced force acts on it. That is why passengers lurch forward when a taxi brakes.
lesson.html: No unbalanced force: no change in motion

lesson.say: Force equals mass times acceleration. The bigger the mass, the more force you need for the same acceleration.
lesson.html: F = m × a

lesson.say: For every force, there is an equal and opposite force on the other object. A rocket pushes gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up.
lesson.html: Action and reaction: equal and opposite

example.q: A 1 000 kg car accelerates at 2 m/s². What resultant force is needed?
steps: F = m × a.

questions.q: What force is needed to accelerate a 50 kg trolley at 3 m/s², in newtons?
A 10 N force acts on a 2 kg mass. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
Why do passengers lurch forward when a taxi brakes suddenly?
options: Their bodies keep moving forward (the first law)
questions.explain: Their bodies keep moving until a force (a seatbelt) stops them.

questions.q: A swimmer pushes the water backwards. What happens?
options: The water pushes the swimmer forwards
The water pushes the swimmer down
questions.explain: The water pushes back on the swimmer with an equal, opposite force.

questions.q: Which law is F = ma?
hints: It links force, mass and acceleration.
Not the first or the third.
questions.explain: F = ma is Newton's second law.

units.parent: Your child used Newton's laws to explain everyday motion.
units.teacher: Criterion A: applies Newton's three laws to explain everyday motion and uses F = ma quantitatively.
units.done: Forces change motion; F = ma; every force has an equal, opposite partner.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Explaining a pattern
units.caps: IEB Mathematics (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 10 number patterns, with emphasis on generalising and justifying in unfamiliar contexts
units.intention: Today I am finding a rule for a pattern and explaining why it works.
units.prompt: How do you know a pattern will continue?

lesson.say: IEB papers often set problems you have never seen before. Start by trying small cases, record them in a table, and look for what changes each time.
lesson.html: Try small cases→Make a table→Spot the change

lesson.say: Matchstick squares in a row: 1 square uses 4 matches, 2 squares use 7, 3 squares use 10. Each new square adds 3, so the rule is 3n plus 1.
lesson.html:
Squares: 1, 2, 3 → matches: 4, 7, 10

Rule: 3n + 1

lesson.say: A rule is stronger when you explain it from the picture. The first square needs one extra match to start, and each square then adds 3 new matches.
lesson.html: Explain the rule from the structure, not only from the numbers.

example.q: Using 3n + 1, how many matches make 20 squares in a row?
steps: Substitute n = 20.
61 matches.

questions.q: Using 3n + 1, how many matches make 10 squares in a row?
A pattern goes 5, 9, 13, 17. What is the next term?
questions.explain: Each term adds 4: 17 + 4 = 21.

questions.q: Which rule gives 5, 9, 13, 17, …?
hints: The difference is 4, so start with 4n.

questions.q: With 3n + 1, how many squares can you make with exactly 100 matches?
Why is explaining the rule from the picture stronger than only checking numbers?
options: It shows why the rule always works, not just for the cases tried
hints: A few cases could be a coincidence.
questions.explain: Explaining from the structure shows the rule works for every case.

units.parent: Your child found and explained the rule behind a pattern, as IEB papers ask.
units.teacher: Shows generalising linear patterns, solving for n, and justifying a rule from the structure of the problem.
units.done: Try small cases, find the rule, then explain why it works.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Justifying in geometry
units.caps: IEB Mathematics (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 10 Euclidean geometry, with emphasis on giving reasons for every statement
units.intention: Today I am writing geometry answers with a reason for every step.
units.prompt: Why might a correct answer still lose marks?

lesson.say: In geometry, every statement needs a reason. Write the statement, then the reason in brackets, using the accepted wording.
lesson.html: ∠A = 70° (vertically opposite ∠s)

lesson.say: Angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees. Angles in a triangle add up to 180 degrees. With parallel lines, alternate angles are equal and co-interior angles add up to 180 degrees.
lesson.html: ∠s on a str line→∠s in a △→alt ∠s, AB ∥ CD→co-int ∠s

lesson.say: In unfamiliar diagrams, work forwards from what you know. Each new angle you find, with its reason, can unlock the next one.
lesson.html: Known → reason → new angle → reason → answer

example.q: AB ∥ CD. A transversal makes ∠1 = 65° at AB. Find the alternate angle at CD.
steps: The lines are parallel.
Alternate angles are equal.
The angle is 65° (alt ∠s, AB ∥ CD).

questions.q: Two angles on a straight line: one is 125°. Find the other, in degrees.
hints: Angles on a straight line add to 180°.

questions.q: A triangle has angles of 50° and 60°. Find the third angle, in degrees.
hints: Angles in a triangle add to 180°.

questions.q: AB ∥ CD and co-interior angles are x and 110°. What is x?
questions.explain: x = 70° (co-int ∠s, AB ∥ CD).

questions.q: Which answer earns full marks?
questions.explain: It gives the statement and the accepted reason.

questions.q: When must you state that lines are parallel in your reason?
options: When using alternate, corresponding or co-interior angles
hints: Some angle facts only work with parallel lines.
questions.explain: These angle facts depend on the lines being parallel.

options: Writing a reason for each step
Working forwards from what I know

units.parent: Your child practised giving a reason for every step in geometry.
units.teacher: Shows using angle relationships with correctly stated reasons and constructing chains of reasoning in unfamiliar diagrams.
units.done: Every statement needs a reason, in the accepted wording.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Reading a visual source
units.caps: IEB English Home Language (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 10 visual literacy, with emphasis on irony and critical comment in unseen sources
units.intention: Today I am analysing how a cartoon uses irony to criticise.
units.prompt: Have you seen a cartoon that made a serious point?
units.passage:
Source: a cartoon, described (a 2to.iQ text)

A huge billboard reads "SAVE WATER. SAVE LIVES." Beneath it, a sprinkler is watering the billboard company's perfect green lawn at midday. A thin learner walks past carrying two buckets from a communal tap. The caption reads: "We're all in this together."

lesson.say: Read the source, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Source: a cartoon, described (a 2to.iQ text)

A huge billboard reads "SAVE WATER. SAVE LIVES." Beneath it, a sprinkler is watering the billboard company's perfect green lawn at midday. A thin learner walks past carrying two buckets from a communal tap. The caption reads: "We're all in this together."

lesson.say: Irony is when what is said or shown is the opposite of what is really happening. The billboard says save water, while the company wastes water on its lawn.
lesson.html: Message: save water. Reality: wasting water.

lesson.say: Satire uses humour or irony to criticise. Here the target is the company, and anyone who preaches to others while doing the opposite.
lesson.html: Target→Technique→Message

example.q: Explain the irony of the caption 'We're all in this together.'
steps: The caption claims everyone shares the burden.
The cartoon shows the company wasting water while a poor learner carries buckets.
The caption is ironic: they are clearly not in it together.

questions.q: What is the main target of the cartoon's criticism?
hints: Who is doing the opposite of what they say?
questions.explain: The company preaches saving water while wasting it.

questions.q: Why is the sprinkler running at midday significant?
options: Most water evaporates then, so it is especially wasteful
hints: What happens to water in the midday heat?
questions.explain: Watering at midday wastes the most water.

questions.q: What does the contrast between the green lawn and the learner with buckets suggest?
options: Inequality in who carries the burden of saving water
questions.explain: It highlights unequal access and burden.

questions.q: What is satire?
options: Using humour or irony to criticise
questions.explain: Satire criticises through humour or irony.

questions.q: Which answer best analyses the caption?
options: The caption is ironic, because the cartoon shows the burden falls unequally.
The caption says we are together.
There is a caption at the bottom.
questions.explain: It names the technique and explains its effect.

units.parent: Your child analysed how a cartoon uses irony to criticise.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting visual texts, identifying irony and satirical targets, and analysing contrasts in unseen sources.
units.done: Find the contrast, name the target, and explain the irony.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Language, bias and manipulation
units.caps: IEB English Home Language (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 10 critical language awareness: bias, emotive language and manipulation
units.intention: Today I am spotting how language is used to persuade and manipulate.
units.prompt: How can the same event be told in two very different ways?
units.passage:
Source: from a community newspaper editorial (a 2to.iQ text)

The so-called experts want us to believe that load-shedding schedules are fair. Ordinary residents know better. Every week, the leafy suburbs seem to get their power back first, while our township waits in the dark. It is time for the municipality to stop hiding behind spreadsheets and tell us the truth.

lesson.say: Read the source, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Source: from a community newspaper editorial (a 2to.iQ text)

The so-called experts want us to believe that load-shedding schedules are fair. Ordinary residents know better. Every week, the leafy suburbs seem to get their power back first, while our township waits in the dark. It is time for the municipality to stop hiding behind spreadsheets and tell us the truth.

lesson.say: Writers choose words that carry feelings. Calling people the so-called experts mocks them, and waits in the dark makes us feel sympathy.
lesson.html: so-called experts→waits in the dark→hiding behind spreadsheets

lesson.say: Ask what evidence is given. The word seem shows the writer has an impression, not proof. Strong criticism needs facts.
lesson.html: Ask: what is the evidence?

example.q: What is the effect of 'hiding behind spreadsheets'?
steps: Hiding suggests dishonesty.
Spreadsheets suggests cold numbers instead of people.
It makes the municipality seem secretive and uncaring.

questions.q: What does 'so-called experts' suggest?
questions.explain: 'So-called' mocks and doubts their status.

questions.q: Which word shows the writer has an impression, not proof?
hints: Look at 'seem to get their power back first'.
questions.explain: 'Seem' signals an impression, not evidence.

questions.q: What would most strengthen the writer's argument?
options: Data comparing outage hours in different areas
questions.explain: Facts and figures would support the claim.

questions.q: 'Ordinary residents know better' appeals to…
options: a sense of shared identity against the experts
questions.explain: It builds a shared 'us' against the experts.

questions.q: Which statement is most balanced?
options: Some residents believe the schedule favours certain areas, and want the data published.
hints: Balanced means fair to both sides.
questions.explain: It reports the concern without loaded language.

units.parent: Your child spotted bias and emotive language in an editorial.
units.teacher: Shows identifying loaded and emotive language, distinguishing evidence from impression, and producing balanced alternatives.
units.done: Spot the loaded words, ask for evidence, and say it fairly.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Reading a scientific source
units.caps: IEB Life Sciences (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 10 scientific skills: reading and interpreting graphs in unseen sources
units.intention: Today I am reading a graph carefully and describing the trend.
units.prompt: What do you look at first on a graph?

lesson.say: Start with the title, the axes, the units and the scale. Many marks are lost by misreading the scale.
lesson.html: Title→Axes and units→Scale→Trend

lesson.say: Describe the overall pattern and give data from the graph. For example: as temperature increases from 10 to 35 degrees Celsius, the rate of photosynthesis increases from 4 to 20 units.
lesson.html: Trend + data from the graph

lesson.say: If the question asks you to explain, give the biological reason, not only the pattern. Enzymes work faster as temperature increases, up to their optimum.
lesson.html: Describe = what. Explain = why.

example.q: A graph shows heart rate rising from 70 to 140 beats per minute during 5 minutes of exercise. Describe and explain.
steps: Describe: heart rate doubles, from 70 to 140 beats per minute.
Explain: muscles need more oxygen and glucose during exercise.
So the heart pumps faster to deliver more blood.

questions.q: What should you check first on a graph?
options: The title, axes, units and scale
questions.explain: Understanding the axes and scale prevents misreading.

questions.q: Which is the best description of a trend?
options: As temperature increases from 10 °C to 35 °C, the rate increases from 4 to 20 units.
questions.explain: It describes the pattern and quotes data.

questions.q: A question says 'explain the trend'. What must you include?
options: The biological reason for the pattern
questions.explain: Explaining needs a biological reason.

questions.q: Heart rate rises from 70 to 140 beats per minute. By how many beats per minute did it increase?
questions.explain: 140 − 70 = 70 beats per minute.

questions.q: On a graph, each small square on the y-axis is 2 units, not 1. What is the risk?
options: Reading values wrongly if you assume 1 unit per square
questions.explain: Assuming the wrong scale gives wrong readings.

units.parent: Your child practised reading graphs carefully and explaining trends.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting axes and scales, describing trends with data, and distinguishing description from explanation.
units.done: Check the axes and scale, describe with data, then explain with biology.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Planning an investigation
units.caps: IEB Life Sciences (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 10 scientific investigation: aim, hypothesis, variables, validity and reliability
units.intention: Today I am planning a valid and reliable investigation.
units.prompt: How would you test whether music helps plants grow?

lesson.say: The aim says what you are investigating. The hypothesis is a prediction you can test. For example: seeds kept at 25 degrees Celsius will germinate faster than seeds kept at 10 degrees Celsius.
lesson.html: Aim: to investigate… · Hypothesis: a testable prediction

lesson.say: An investigation is valid if it tests what it claims to. Change only one variable, and keep everything else the same.
lesson.html: Valid: tests the right thing, fairly.

lesson.say: Results are reliable if they can be repeated. Use large samples and repeat the investigation, then calculate averages.
lesson.html: Reliable: repeat and use large samples.

example.q: Plan: does temperature affect how fast seeds germinate?
steps: Independent: temperature. Dependent: time to germinate.
Fixed: the type of seed, the amount of water, light and soil.
Use 20 seeds at each temperature and repeat, to improve reliability.

questions.q: Which is a testable hypothesis?
options: Seeds at 25 °C will germinate faster than seeds at 10 °C.
questions.explain: It predicts a measurable result.

questions.q: Using 20 seeds instead of 2 mainly improves…
questions.explain: Large samples make results more reliable.

questions.q: Keeping light and water the same for all seeds improves…
questions.explain: Controlling variables makes the test valid.

questions.q: What is the dependent variable when testing temperature on germination?
questions.explain: You measure the time to germinate.

questions.q: Why repeat the investigation?
options: To check the results are consistent
hints: Will you get the same result?
questions.explain: Repeating checks that results are consistent.

options: Choosing what to keep the same

units.parent: Your child planned a fair, repeatable science investigation.
units.teacher: Shows formulating aims and hypotheses, identifying variables, and distinguishing validity from reliability.
units.done: Valid: test the right thing fairly. Reliable: repeat with large samples.

units.subject: Advanced Programme Mathematics
units.title: Absolute value
units.caps: IEB Advanced Programme Mathematics: Module 1, Algebra (absolute value: equations and inequalities)
units.intention: Today I am solving equations with absolute value.
units.prompt: How far is −5 from 0?

lesson.say: The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero, so it is never negative. The absolute value of minus 5 is 5.
If the absolute value of x minus 3 equals 4, then x minus 3 is 4 or minus 4. So x is 7 or minus 1.
If the absolute value of x is less than 2, then x is within 2 of zero. So x is between minus 2 and 2.

example.q: Solve |2x + 1| = 5.
steps: x = 2 or x = −3.

questions.q: What is |−8|?
Solve |x| = 6.
questions.explain: Both 6 and −6 are 6 units from 0.

questions.q: Solve |x − 3| = 4.
questions.explain: x = 7 or x = −1.

questions.q: Solve |x| < 2.
questions.explain: x lies between −2 and 2.

questions.q: Solve |x + 1| = −3.
hints: Can an absolute value be negative?
questions.explain: An absolute value can't equal a negative number.

units.parent: Your child solved equations and inequalities with absolute value.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting absolute value as distance, solving absolute value equations by cases and solving simple inequalities.
units.done: Absolute value is distance: split into two cases, and it is never negative.
